u1-emuA:
Comment #31675 On one hand, to experiment with a different way of doing things, it doesn't necessarily have to involve everyone, or even buying land. People could try it first in some more contained context in the parent group, then maybe in a semi-autonomous way, then maybe as a seed group close by that is connected in a few ways (shared tool library, child care, businesses, friendships, etc.) Splitting off entirely is just one point on a gradient of connectedness, and shouldn't be required in order to experiment.

On the other hand, some experiments (like different land systems, for example) can't be tested in a way that is cheap and will also give useful information. If the land system implies a different population, and different rules, trying to test it in a way that is not supportive of those rules and population is likely to give bad results.
u1-emuB:
If one of the first responses to "what if we tried it a different way" is not "some of us will go buy some land and try it", but first "we'll try it in this group", then "we'll try it in a semi-autonomous way, still part of this group", then "we'll split off to nearby land and share some things like tools, child care, business, friendships, etc", then "we'll split off completely" is just one step along a gradient of splitting off to try new ideas, and people don't feel they have to split off in order to try new ideas.

It may be that some experiments (like trying a different set of rules about land, or having a different population, or any number of rules that interact) are hard to try without trying them in a way that isn't cheap.
u2-emuA:
The communities need a way to connect and spread, without turning into a super commune (that's essentially just a state). I'd like to help them connect, but also be distinct so that they can learn from one another. How can they spread their presence, help each other, allow for travel between themselves, etc?

At a federation level I see the need to spread out, to send out people to help heal, to learn, to spread the seed, etc. It's also important to keep from getting too comfortable and forgetting that the enclave isn't the whole.
u2-emuB:
They do need to be solved in some way if the idea is for the communities to spread, while not becoming a super-commune. But they should be solved in a way that encourages movement between communities and help between communities, and also keeps the differences alive.

For example, part of what a federation can do is spread the word about what is being done to help people heal, train people and seed new projects etc. Also, it could be a way to keep people from existing enclaves from thinking that they are the whole movement.
u3-emuA: This is a good warning, especially as the Federation of Egalitarian Communities re-builds. It takes work to run a federation. Delegates. Records. Compliance. Coordinating resources. Holding meetings. Succession. Doing some sort of dispute function. These things all take up labor and material capacity before any actual crises that need to be faced on a local level. If the legal or economic environment requires it, the federation also needs to have a budget of outside money. It might also be good to know that the work of federation does not have to be done by a single entity. Two communities might want to be closely linked as friends. That does not preclude both of those communities from also participating in a general federation. Also, there might be local clusters, or single-function institutions, like the present PEACH health pool, which is not currently governed by the FEC delegates.
u3-emuB: (NOTE: It may be good to be aware that the Federation of Egalitarian Communities is now in the process of rebuilding. Federation work is work. Delegates, records, administrative compliance work, coordinating and making available federation resources, holding federation meetings, succession planning, functioning as a dispute body, etc., all take up a good deal of labor and material capacity, even before real crises emerge at the local level. In most legal/economic systems, a federation will need a budget of “outside” money to function. These functions can be divided among more than one federation body, if desired. Two communities can be friends with each other without being members of a more general federation. Local clusters are one possibility; functional clusters are another possibility (e.g., the PEACH health pool, currently not governed by FEC delegates).)
u4-emuA: An important point should also be made that cooperation should not mean assimilation. In the FEC, in addition to communities that are full members, or are working towards membership, there will also be Friends who will likely always be merely Friends. It will be necessary to provide for freedom of movement between these communities, in theory, if not in practice. It will also be necessary to deal with all of the issues, both mundane and subtle, which arise when members move from one community to another. It is likely that these will require the creation of interfaces, however thin.
u4-emuB: On a related point, the desire to cooperate without merging makes sense to . The FEC has full members, communities working towards becoming full members, and friends who may or may not ever want to become members. Freedom of movement should exist between these communities in theory. In practice it requires agreements and interfaces that define housing, status, healthcare, record transfer, labor, travel, taxes, and arbitration in the case of a community not wanting to let a person go. These interfaces can be very thin.
u5-emuA: Even if some communities don’t use money internally, they will still probably want a way to keep track of exchanges and obligations. Gifts, shared resources (food, medicine, vehicles, tools), trades of labor, temporary housing, “social” visits (that are really for training or connection purposes), building events, and many other types of events may or may not create future obligations. It will be useful for the federation to keep track of these for each purpose, without needing to ascribe a value or require the exchange to be “even”. If cash is used for transactions with the outside world, it will also be important for communities to keep the federation’s use of cash separate from its other activities. Grants, loans, loan guarantees, shared enterprise commitments, and other forms of financial exchange are all different, and should be tracked separately. All of the communities will not be liable for all of the federation’s obligations, nor will any community have an unlimited obligation to provide labor, resources, land, or tools to another.
u5-emuB: It’s possible that some of these things might happen without money even internally, but it would help to keep track of them for different purposes. Giving food, medicine, sharing vehicles and tools, exchanging labor, providing emergency housing, building something, visiting for training/relationship building, etc., are all quite different things. Some of them would create an obligation to the other in the future, and some not. And there would be many reasons to keep track of them separately. If cash is used, similarly, separate tracking of what money was sent where as a grant, as a loan, as a guarantee, as a commitment to a shared enterprise, etc., would be valuable. But in no case does solidarity imply unlimited liability for one another, or unlimited access to other’s labor, stores, land, tools, etc.
u6-emuA: When two principles conflict, and a new rule is generated to resolve the conflict, not only store the new rule, but store the conflict itself, along with its circumstances, the two conflicting principles, the first judgment, the reason for the final judgment, any dissent, the consequences, and which version of the rule resolved it. When the rule changes, re-run the case.
u6-emuB: When making a rule from a collision of two principles, store not only the resultant rule but also the original problematic case, including which principles were involved, what original judgments were made regarding the case and those principles, what judgment was ultimately reached and why, if there was dissent from the judgment, what were the consequences of the judgment, and what version of the resultant rule the judgment was made under. When the rule changes, re-run the case.
